Code encoding

Words: 143 Articles: 2
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
Code encoding maps messages injectively to codewords. For a dimension-k linear code with generator matrix G, the standard encoder maps m∈Fqk​ to mG. The redundancy makes error detection and recovery possible; for a Reed-Solomon code, encoding can instead evaluate a message polynomial at the chosen field elements.

Systematic encoding

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Code encoding OurBigBook.com
A systematic encoder retains the message symbols unchanged in designated coordinates of its codeword and calculates the remaining check symbols. For a linear code, choosing an invertible set of k columns of a generator matrix and changing its row basis gives this form.

Systematic polynomial encoding of a cyclic code (c(x)=xn−kM(x)−(xn−kM(x)modg(x)))

Words: 60
Systematic encoding OurBigBook.com
For a length-n, dimension-k cyclic code with generator polynomial g of degree n−k, let the message polynomial satisfy degM<k. Subtracting the remainder upon polynomial division by g makes the displayed word divisible by g. The remainder has degree less than n−k, so the highest k coordinates retain the coefficients of M. This gives systematic encoding without losing any message information.

Gilbert–Varshamov bound

Words: 219 Articles: 3
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
For codes over an alphabet of size q, the greedy packing argument gives Aq​(n,d)≥qn/Vq​(n,d−1), where Vq​(n,r)=∑j=0r​(jn​)(q−1)j. A maximal distance-d code has radius-(d−1) Hamming balls covering the entire space; counting their union proves the lower bound. The linear refinement is the Varshamov bound for linear codes.
// Target: algebra.bigb

Worst-case correction guarantee from the Gilbert–Varshamov bound (R≤1−h2​(2p),0≤p<1/4)

Words: 78
Gilbert–Varshamov bound OurBigBook.com
A binary code rate R is guaranteed with correction of every error pattern of Hamming weight at most t=⌊pN⌋ when R≤1−h2​(2p) and p<1/4. Choose minimum Hamming distance 2t+1. The Gilbert–Varshamov bound and entropy bound for a Hamming ball give at least 2N(1−h2​(2p)) codewords. To deduce vanishing error probability for a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, use strict inequality in the rate condition and a correction radius (p+ε)N; the weak law of large numbers then controls the tail. Correcting exactly the mean number of errors does not by itself ensure reliable transmission.
// Target: algebra.bigb

Asymptotic Gilbert–Varshamov bound (αq​(δ)≥1−Hq​(δ))

Words: 28
Gilbert–Varshamov bound OurBigBook.com
For 0≤δ≤1−1/q, take logarithms of the Gilbert–Varshamov bound and apply the Hamming ball volume exponent. The Varshamov bound for linear codes gives the same achievable lower bound within linear codes for prime-power q.
// Target: algebra.bigb

Varshamov bound for linear codes

Words: 62
Gilbert–Varshamov bound OurBigBook.com
For a prime-power alphabet size q, a linear [n,k,≥d] code exists if Vq​(n−1,d−2)<qn−k. Choose parity-check columns successively, avoiding combinations of at most d−2 earlier columns. Fewer than qn−k vectors are forbidden, so such a choice is possible. No set of at most d−1 columns is dependent, and the resulting kernel has dimension at least k.

Codeword (c∈C)

Words: 73 Articles: 1
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
A codeword is a member of the specified set of words used to encode messages. For a linear code specified by a parity-check matrix H, the codewords are precisely the vectors satisfying Hc=0. The minimum distance between distinct codewords controls error correction.

The codeword length is the number of alphabet symbols in a codeword. For a binary word it counts bits; in a prefix code, it is the depth of the corresponding leaf in the code tree.

Block code

Coding theory OurBigBook.com
A block code assigns source messages to words of a fixed length over an alphabet. Its codewords form a subset of that fixed-length word space; a binary block code uses the two-symbol finite field F2​.

Binary block code

Words: 1k Articles: 29
Block code OurBigBook.com
A binary [n,m,d] code is a set of m distinct words in F2n​ whose minimum pairwise Hamming distance is d. Here n is the block length and m is the number of codewords.

An error-correcting code is a set of codewords chosen with enough separation to detect or correct transmission errors.
Repetition code
Words: 29
Error-correcting code OurBigBook.com
A binary repetition code represents one bit by repeating it a fixed number of times. Majority decoding corrects fewer than half as many bit flips as the block length.

Binary block code OurBigBook.com
The Hamming distance between two equal-length words is the number of coordinates in which they differ.
Hamming space (Hn,q​=Fqn​)
Words: 36
Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
The Hamming space of length n over a finite field Fq​ is the set Fqn​ equipped with Hamming distance, the number of coordinates at which two words differ. The Hamming weight of a word is its distance from zero.
Diameter of a set family (diam(F)=maxA,B∈F​∣A△B∣)
Words: 54
Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
This is the maximum Hamming distance between the characteristic vectors of members of a set family. In a down-set, one can replace a pair by disjoint subsets with the same union, so the maximum distance equals the largest size of a union of two members. A t-intersecting family has diameter at most n−t.
Normalized Hamming distance (dH​(x,y)=dH​(x,y)/n)
Words: 23
Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
On binary words of length n, normalized Hamming distance is the fraction of differing coordinates. Unlike unscaled Hamming distance, it makes the Hamming cubes a Lévy family under uniform probability measures.
Hamming cube ({−1,1}n)
Words: 66 Articles: 1
Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
The Hamming cube is {−1,1}n, or equivalently {0,1}n, equipped with Hamming distance. Under its uniform probability measure, the distance from a fixed vertex has the binomial distribution with parameters n,1/2. This converts geometric ball sizes into probability tails.
Exponential packing of a Hamming cube (∣S∣≥e9n/32,dH​(s,s′)≥n/8)
Words: 31
Hamming cube OurBigBook.com
An inclusion-maximal separated set of separation an covers the Hamming cube by strict-radius an balls. The Hoeffding lower-tail bound for Hamming balls then gives at least e2n(1/2−a)2 selected vertices. At a=1/8 this yields e9n/32 vertices, all separated by at least n/8.
Hamming distance between unlabelled bipartitions (Δ(S,T)=min{∣S△T∣,∣S△Tc∣})
Words: 120 Articles: 1
Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
This Hamming distance on partitions identifies a group with its complement because exchanging the two group names does not change the partition. Complementation is an isometry of the ordinary Hamming distance, so minimizing over this two-element group action gives a quotient metric and preserves the triangle inequality. Negating a zero-one indicator is not complementation; with ±1 membership vectors, it is.
Sign rounding bound for a unit eigenvector (Δ(S,S)≤n∥vv⊤−vv⊤∥F2​)
Words: 65
Hamming distance between unlabelled bipartitions OurBigBook.com
Suppose vi​=±1/n​ encodes the true partition and v is a unit estimated eigenvector. Every coordinate of the wrong sign contributes at least 1/n to minσ=±1​∥v−σv∥22​=2(1−∣v⊤v∣). Since this is at most 2(1−∣v⊤v∣2), which is the squared Frobenius distance between the rank-one orthogonal projection matrices, the bound follows. Coordinates estimated as zero may be assigned consistently to either group.

Hamming distance OurBigBook.com
The Hamming ball of radius r about a word x is the set of words whose Hamming distance from x is at most r.
Hamming ball volume exponent (limn→∞​n−1logq​Vq​(n,⌊ρn⌋)=Hq​(ρ))
Words: 49
Hamming ball OurBigBook.com
For 0≤ρ≤1−1/q, the exponential growth rate of a q-ary Hamming ball is Hq​(ρ). Stirling's formula gives the exponent of each summand (in​)(q−1)i, and the sum lies between its largest term and n+1 times that term. Above the entropy-maximizing radius fraction, the exponent is one.

Hoeffding lower-tail bound for Hamming balls (2−n∣Ban​∣≤e−2n(1/2−a)2)
Words: 49
Hamming ball OurBigBook.com
For a uniform vertex of the Hamming cube, distance from a fixed vertex is the sum of n independent Bernoulli random variables with parameter 1/2. The lower-tail Hoeffding inequality implies that the fraction of vertices at distance at most an, 0<a<1/2, is at most e−2n(1/2−a)2. Strict-radius balls satisfy the same upper bound.
Entropy bound for a Hamming ball (∑j≤ρn​(jn​)≤enh(ρ))
Words: 57
Hamming ball OurBigBook.com
For 0<ρ≤1/2, the number of binary words within Hamming distance ρn of a fixed word is at most enh(ρ), with the binary entropy function in natural logarithms. In 1=∑j​(jn​)ρj(1−ρ)n−j, each summand weight for j≤ρn is at least ρρn(1−ρ)n(1−ρ)=e−nh(ρ). Also h′′(ρ)=−1/(ρ(1−ρ))≤−4, so log2−h(1/2−a)≥2a2. These two bounds give the approximate-recovery denominator in the list-decoding Fano inequality.

Perfect code

Words: 392 Articles: 7
Binary block code OurBigBook.com
A code of minimum distance d is perfect if its Hamming balls of radius ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ partition the ambient word space. Every word then has a unique nearest codeword within the code's error-correction radius.
Binary Golay code (G23​=[23,12,7])
Words: 361 Articles: 6
Perfect code OurBigBook.com
The length-23 binary Golay code is the cyclic code over F2​ generated by
g(X)=1+X+X5+X6+X7+X9+X11.
(1)
It has dimension 12, minimum Hamming distance 7, and its radius-3 Hamming balls partition F223​. Its parity extension has length 24, dimension 12, and minimum Hamming distance 8.
// Target: algebra.bigb
Extended binary Golay code (G24​=[24,12,8])
Words: 220 Articles: 2
Binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
The extended binary Golay code is the parity extension of the length-23 binary Golay code. It is a self-dual code and a doubly even code, with minimum Hamming distance eight. Its radius-three Hamming balls are disjoint but do not cover its Hamming space; it is not a perfect code.
Three-error syndrome decoding of extended Golay code
Words: 79
Extended binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
For a binary symmetric matrix A with A2=I, the syndrome of an error (p,q) relative to the column parity-check matrix (I;A) is s=p+qA. An error of total Hamming weight at most three has at most one nonzero bit in one half. Test s, each s+Ai​, sA, and each sA+Ai​ for weights at most three, two, three and two respectively. These identify (s,0), (s+Ai​,ei​), (0,sA) and (ei​,sA+Ai​). For the extended binary Golay code, minimum Hamming distance eight guarantees that at most one such error exists.
Systematic-matrix proof of extended Golay distance
Words: 106
Extended binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
Suppose a binary symmetric matrix A satisfies A2=I, has one row of Hamming weight eleven and eleven rows of Hamming weight seven, and every sum of two distinct rows has Hamming weight six. Then (I∣A) generates a self-dual code. Its rows have weights twelve or eight; their mutual orthogonality makes every generated word doubly even. A weight-four word (u,uA) would have left-half weight one, two, three or four. The first two cases are excluded by the stated row weights; weight three would force uA to be a unit vector and hence u to be a row of A; weight four would force uA=0. Thus weight four is impossible and the minimum Hamming distance is eight.
Golay generator polynomial
Words: 6
Binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
The generator polynomial of a cyclic code defining the binary Golay code is 1+X+X5+X6+X7+X9+X11.
BCH and parity-extension proof of the binary Golay distance
Words: 49
Binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
A root β of the binary Golay generator polynomial has order 23, and the Frobenius endomorphism shows that β,β2,β3,β4 are roots: 28≡3(mod23). The BCH bound gives minimum Hamming distance at least five. The circular autocorrelation of the binary Golay generator makes its parity extension doubly even, excluding original weights five and six. The generator itself has Hamming weight seven, proving that the distance is exactly seven.
// Target: algebra.bigb
Circular autocorrelation of the binary Golay generator
Words: 48
Binary Golay code OurBigBook.com
The polynomial identity (X+1)g(X)grev(X)=X23+1, where grev(X)=X11g(X−1), implies
g(X)g(X−1)≡1+X+⋯+X22(modX23−1).
(2)
Every coefficient is the binary inner product of the coefficient vector of g with one cyclic shift. Thus every such inner product is one. Appending a parity bit to the cyclic shifts gives mutually orthogonal weight-eight vectors, so orthogonal generators of doubly even codes applies.

Punctured code

Puncturing (coding theory) OurBigBook.com
Puncturing a code at one coordinate deletes that coordinate from every codeword. For a code of minimum distance d≥2, puncturing preserves its number of words and gives minimum distance d or d−1.

One-time pad

Words: 146 Articles: 3
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
For messages in a finite additive group, a one-time pad encrypts X as C=X+K, where the key K is uniform and independent of X, as long as the message, and never reused. Then C is uniform and independent of X, giving perfect secrecy.

Two-time pad attack

Words: 47
One-time pad OurBigBook.com
If two plaintexts are encrypted by adding the same one-time-pad key, subtracting the ciphertexts cancels the key and reveals the difference of the plaintexts. Redundancy in natural language or another structured message space can then reveal both messages, so a one-time pad must never reuse key material.

Perfect secrecy

Words: 23
One-time pad OurBigBook.com
An encryption scheme has perfect secrecy when the ciphertext and plaintext are independent random variables, so observing the ciphertext does not change the plaintext's probability distribution.

Malleability of an additive one-time pad

Words: 33
One-time pad OurBigBook.com
If an interceptor knows that an additive one-time-pad ciphertext C encrypts plaintext P and wants it to decrypt as P′, replacing it by
C′=C−P+P′
(5)
works without knowing the key, since C′=P′+K.

Secret sharing

Words: 150 Articles: 3
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
A secret-sharing scheme distributes shares of a secret so that authorized collections can reconstruct it while unauthorized collections reveal no information about it.

Threshold secret sharing

Words: 127 Articles: 2
Secret sharing OurBigBook.com
An (r,s) threshold secret-sharing scheme issues s shares: every collection of at least r shares reconstructs the secret, while every collection of fewer than r shares has a distribution independent of the secret.

Shamir's secret sharing

Words: 94 Articles: 1
Threshold secret sharing OurBigBook.com
Shamir's secret sharing places a secret N at the constant term of a random polynomial f∈Fp​[X] of degree at most r−1 and issues distinct nonzero evaluation pairs (xi​,f(xi​)). Any r shares recover f by polynomial interpolation. Given fewer than r shares, every candidate constant term has the same number of compatible coefficient tuples, which gives perfect secrecy.
Perfect secrecy of Shamir's threshold scheme
Words: 36
Shamir's secret sharing OurBigBook.com
Conditioned on any r−1 shares in Shamir's secret sharing, each candidate secret in Fp​ remains equally likely. Appending (0,N) to those shares determines exactly one degree-at-most-(r−1) polynomial for every candidate N, by the nonzero Vandermonde determinant.

Discrete memoryless channel

Words: 153 Articles: 4
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
A discrete memoryless channel has finite input and output alphabets and transition probabilities P(y∣x). Conditional on the input symbols, different channel uses have independent outputs governed by the same transition probabilities.

Words: 68 Articles: 1

A finite-alphabet erasure channel transmits the input symbol unchanged with probability 1−f and replaces it by a distinct erasure flag with probability f, independently of the symbol. Output sets of different-length linear-feedback registers

Words: 92
Linear-feedback shift register OurBigBook.com
Under the convention that a register emits each shifted-out symbol, its first d output symbols are exactly its initial fill. Thus a binary register of length d has 2d−1 distinct outputs from nonzero fills. For lengths r<s, at least one longer-register output is absent from the shorter register, guaranteeing a pair of unequal nonzero outputs. The two sets need not be disjoint: recurrences sn+1​=sn​ and sn+2​=sn​ both generate constant ones. Nor must they intersect: the length-one recurrence and sn+2​=sn+1​+sn​ have no common nonzero output, since constant ones fail the second recurrence.

The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm finds the shortest linear recurrence satisfied by a finite sequence over a field. It processes symbols incrementally, updating the connection polynomial whenever the current recurrence has a nonzero discrepancy.

Minimum recurrence length after a new discrepancy (L′≥r+1−L)

Words: 111
Berlekamp-Massey algorithm OurBigBook.com
Suppose a connection polynomial C of degree at most L, with recurrence span L gives zero recurrence discrepancies through index r−1 but a nonzero discrepancy at r. If a polynomial D of span L′ successfully explains the prefix through r and L+L′≤r, evaluate the coefficient at r in the convolution (CD)x. Applying D first makes it zero. Applying C first leaves its nonzero discrepancy at r, because the earlier discrepancies vanish and D has constant coefficient one. This contradiction gives the displayed lower bound. It is the minimality step used by the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm; the algorithm cancels the new discrepancy with a shifted earlier failed polynomial.

Linear code OurBigBook.com
For distinct elements a1​,…,an​ of a finite field, a Reed-Solomon code consists of the evaluation vectors (f(a1​),…,f(an​)) of polynomials with degree less than k. It has dimension k and minimum Hamming distance n−k+1, so it is a maximum distance separable code. A nonzero polynomial has at most its degree many distinct polynomial roots. Primitive cyclic Reed-Solomon codes use all nonzero field elements, ordered as powers of a primitive root of unity; arbitrary evaluation sets need not give a cyclic code.

Binary linear code OurBigBook.com
A length-n, dimension-k binary linear code has full support when no coordinate vanishes on every codeword, equivalently when the union of the supports of a vector of all codewords covers every coordinate. Every coordinate is then a nonzero linear functional on the message vector space F2k​. Translation by a vector on which it is one pairs the zero and one fibers, so exactly 2k−1 codewords contribute one in that coordinate. Summing these contributions proves the formula. If there are r nonzero columns in a full-rank generator matrix, the same argument gives r2k−1 instead.

Ordered weight-three supports of a vector are determined by two distinct nonzero vectors, giving n(n−1) choices. For weight four, the third vector must avoid the three nonzero vectors in the linear span of the first two, giving n(n−1)(n−3) choices. For weight five, the first three must be linearly independent, and the fourth must avoid all seven nonzero vectors in their linear span, giving n(n−1)(n−3)(n−7) choices. The final vector is their sum. Dividing by 3!, 4!, and 5! counts unordered supports of a vector and proves the displayed weight enumerator coefficients.

Extended Hamming code ([8,4,4])

Words: 60
Hamming code OurBigBook.com
Adding an overall parity bit to the Hamming code of length seven gives an eight-bit linear code with minimum Hamming distance four: every resulting weight is even, every original nonzero weight is at least three, and a weight-three word extends to weight four. Thus it detects up to three errors when testing codeword membership and corrects one error. Joint single-error correction and double-error detection uses the overall parity together with the seven-bit syndrome.

Hamming code of length seven ([7,4,3])

Words: 54
Hamming code OurBigBook.com
The binary linear code known as the Hamming code of length seven is the kernel of a 3×7 parity-check matrix whose columns are all the nonzero vectors of F23​. Its dimension is four. No one-column or two-column sum vanishes, but some three-column sum does, so its minimum Hamming distance is three. The syndrome of a one-bit error is its column, uniquely identifying the erroneous position.

Binary simplex code

Words: 101 Articles: 1
Hamming code OurBigBook.com
The binary simplex code is the dual of the binary Hamming code. For redundancy r it has parameters [2r−1,r,2r−1].
Its relation to the Hamming code is duality, not equality of the code families.
Constant weight of a binary simplex code (wt(aH)=2l−1(a=0))
Words: 69
Binary simplex code OurBigBook.com
When the columns of H are every nonzero vector in F2l​, a nonzero row vector a defines a nonzero linear functional v↦a⋅v. Exactly half the 2l input vectors take value 1: translation by any vector on which the functional is 1 pairs its zero and one fibres. Removing the zero input removes only a zero value. Thus every nonzero word in the binary simplex code has Hamming weight 2l−1.

Perfectness of a Hamming code

Words: 41
Hamming code OurBigBook.com
A Hamming code has 22r−r−1 words, and each radius-one Hamming ball contains 1+(2r−1)=2r vectors. Its minimum distance is three, so these balls are disjoint, and their total size is 22r−1. They therefore partition the ambient space, making the code perfect.

Minimum-distance error-detection and correction guarantee

Words: 40
Linear code OurBigBook.com
A code of minimum Hamming distance d detects every pattern of at most d−1 errors and uniquely corrects every pattern of at most ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors. The correction claim follows because Hamming balls of that radius around distinct codewords are disjoint.

Coding theory OurBigBook.com
A length-n cyclic code over Fq​ is an ideal of Fq​[X]/(Xn−1). It is generated by a monic divisor of Xn−1.

Words: 33
Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
A linear code is negacyclic if (c0​,…,cn−1​) being a codeword implies that (−cn−1​,c0​,…,cn−2​) is a codeword. Polynomial identification makes it an ideal modulo Xn+1. For odd n, the substitution X↦−X gives a monomial equivalence of linear codes between negacyclic and cyclic codes.

Zero of a cyclic code

Words: 37
Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
A zero of a cyclic code is a polynomial root of its generator polynomial, taken in a splitting field. Every codeword, represented as a polynomial, vanishes there. For a repeated-root cyclic code, the multiplicity of a root must also be retained: ordinary evaluations alone need not determine the code.

Repeated-root cyclic code

Words: 141 Articles: 2
Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
A repeated-root cyclic code has length divisible by the characteristic of its field, so the polynomial XN−1 has repeated factors. Its generator can involve powers of those factors. In characteristic two, length 2t gives X2t+1=(X+1)2t.

Repeated-root parity-check matrix

Words: 57
Repeated-root cyclic code OurBigBook.com
If the generator polynomial of a cyclic code has distinct roots αi​ with multiplicities mi​, a word belongs to the code exactly when c[ℓ](αi​)=0 for 0≤ℓ<mi​, where c[ℓ] is its Hasse derivative. The corresponding rows have entries (ℓj​)αij−ℓ​ for j≥ℓ and zero otherwise. Expansion in a basis of the splitting field gives equations over the original finite field; an independent selection has rank ∑i​mi​.

Binary cyclic codes of length a power of two

Words: 45
Repeated-root cyclic code OurBigBook.com
For N=2t, the binary cyclic codes are exactly the nested ideals generated by (X+1)j for 0≤j≤N. They have dimensions N−j and canonical check polynomials (X+1)N−j. The endpoint ideals are the entire word space and the zero code.

Check polynomial of a cyclic code (h(X)=(XN−1)/g(X))

Words: 74
Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
For a cyclic code with monic generator g∣XN−1, the canonical check polynomial is h=(XN−1)/g. A word a belongs to the code exactly when ah is zero modulo XN−1, since cancellation in the polynomial ring turns this condition into g∣a. The kernel condition alone allows additional polynomials: it is equivalent to gcd(h,XN−1)=h. Requiring the monic divisor of the modulus singles out the canonical choice.

Binary cyclic codes of length five

Words: 63
Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
Over F2​, X5−1=(X+1)(X4+X3+X2+X+1) and the degree-four factor is irreducible: it has no linear root and is not divisible by the sole irreducible quadratic X2+X+1. The four monic divisors give precisely four cyclic codes: the full five-dimensional space, the four-dimensional even-weight code, the one-dimensional repetition code, and the zero code. Their generator polynomials of a cyclic code are respectively 1, X+1, X4+X3+X2+X+1, and X5−1.

The unique monic divisor g(X) of Xn−1 generating a cyclic code is its generator polynomial. The code has dimension n−degg.

Let α be a root of the generator polynomial of a cyclic code g(X). Every codeword c(X) satisfies c(α)=0, so a received word r=c+e satisfies r(α)=e(α). For a single-symbol error e(X)=aXj, the evaluation r(α)=aαj identifies its value and position when the relevant powers of α are distinct.

Words: 71
Root-evaluation syndrome for a cyclic code OurBigBook.com
For a binary cyclic code with defining zeros of a cyclic code α and α3, a single error in coordinate j has polynomial Xj and syndromes S1​=αj, S3​=α3j. If S1​=0 and S3​=S13​, recover j from the exponent of S1​, flip that coordinate, and verify that the resulting polynomial vanishes at both roots. When the linear code has minimum Hamming distance at least five, this verified correction is the unique codeword within two errors. The syndrome relation alone should not replace checking the corrected word.

Cyclic code OurBigBook.com
Given a primitive nth root α, a BCH code of design distance δ has a generator polynomial vanishing at δ−1 consecutive powers αb,…,αb+δ−2.

Designed distance (d(C)≥δ)

Words: 37
BCH code OurBigBook.com
The designed distance of a BCH code is the value δ specified by requiring δ−1 consecutive defining zeros of a cyclic code. The BCH bound guarantees minimum Hamming distance at least δ, but the actual minimum Hamming distance can be larger. To prove equality, one can exhibit a nonzero codeword of Hamming weight exactly δ.

Binary cyclotomic coset modulo an odd integer (Ci​={i,2i,4i,…}(modn))

Words: 77
BCH code OurBigBook.com
For odd n, multiplication by two permutes the residues modulo n. Its orbit through i is the binary cyclotomic coset modulo an odd integer. If α has order n in a finite field whose field characteristic is two, the Frobenius automorphism sends αi to α2i. Hence the minimal polynomial of an algebraic element αi over F2​ is ∏j∈Ci​​(X−αj). Its coefficients are fixed by Frobenius and lie in F2​, and its degree is the orbit size. Thus a binary cyclic code containing one defining zero of a cyclic code must contain the full orbit as zeros.

A Chien search finds error positions by evaluating an error locator polynomial at every possible inverse location value ω−j. A zero identifies coordinate j. Using the recurrence between successive powers of ω avoids recomputing all monomials from scratch.

Rabin cryptosystem

Words: 235 Articles: 4
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
Rabin encryption sends m to m2 modulo a product of two secret primes. Decryption computes the four square roots by the Chinese remainder theorem.

Repeated-message attack on the Rabin cryptosystem (m2modN, m2modN′)

Words: 68
Rabin cryptosystem OurBigBook.com
For coprime moduli N,N′ and 0<m<min(N,N′), the Chinese remainder theorem recovers the integer m2 uniquely in [0,NN′) from the two ciphertexts. An ordinary integer square root then recovers the message. If distinct semiprime moduli share a factor, their greatest common divisor instead reveals factors of both moduli. Learning one message in the coprime case does not by itself give a general factoring algorithm or a decryption key for other ciphertexts.

If N=pq and x2≡y2(modN) while x≡±y(modN), then
N∣(x−y)(x+y),

and gcd(x−y,N) is a nontrivial factor of N.

Square-root oracle reduction for Rabin encryption (P(y≡±xmodN)=1/2)

Words: 78
Factorization from distinct square roots modulo a semiprime OurBigBook.com
For N=pq with distinct odd primes, choose a uniform unit x and give only x2modN to an oracle returning any square root y. Conditional on this square, x is uniform among four roots and independent of the oracle's choice. With probability one half, y is not ±x, and gcd(x−y,N) is a nontrivial factor. Thus full inversion of the squaring map yields randomized integer factorization; this reduction does not equate arbitrary partial leakage with full inversion.

Chosen-square attack on Rabin authentication

Words: 43
Factorization from distinct square roots modulo a semiprime OurBigBook.com
If a purported authentication service returns a square root of every chosen square modulo a Rabin modulus, a verifier who knows one root obtains a different root with substantial probability and can factor the modulus. Repeating the challenge therefore reveals the private key.

Diffie-Hellman key exchange

Words: 115 Articles: 1
Coding theory OurBigBook.com
Alice publishes ga and Bob publishes gb in a public cyclic group; each can then compute the shared secret gab. Its security relies on the difficulty of recovering the exponents or otherwise solving the computational Diffie--Hellman problem.

Multilateral Diffie-Hellman key exchange

Words: 77
Diffie-Hellman key exchange OurBigBook.com
In a cyclic group with generator g, n participants with secret exponents aj​ can exchange n tokens around a ring. Token j starts at gaj​ and is successively exponentiated by its next n−2 recipients before being sent to the final recipient, whose exponent is the only one missing. That recipient completes the exponentiation locally. Each token makes n−1 transmissions, and everyone obtains g∏j​aj​. Thus n(n−1) transmitted group elements suffice. As with two-party Diffie-Hellman key exchange, authentication is needed.

Unique decodability

Coding theory OurBigBook.com
Unique decodability means that every encoded message has at most one decomposition into codewords.

Decipherable code

Words: 570 Articles: 15
Unique decodability OurBigBook.com
A code is decipherable, or uniquely decodable, when every finite concatenation of codewords has at most one decomposition into source codewords.

Suffix code

Words: 41
Decipherable code OurBigBook.com
A decipherable code is suffix-free when no codeword is a proper suffix of another. Reversing all its words gives a prefix code. Consequently it is uniquely decipherable: read a concatenation from the right, where the last codeword is determined uniquely, and continue by induction.

Optimal source code (min∑a​pa​ℓa​)

Words: 35
Decipherable code OurBigBook.com
For a fixed source distribution and code alphabet, an optimal uniquely decodable code minimizes expected codeword length. Huffman coding gives an optimal binary prefix code, and the equivalence of attainable uniquely-decodable and prefix-code lengths gives the same minimum for both classes.

Prefix code

Words: 473 Articles: 12
Decipherable code OurBigBook.com
In a prefix code no codeword is the prefix of another, so concatenated messages have unique instantaneous decoding.
Prefix code for a rare geometric success (EL=n+(1−(1−2−n)2n)−1)
Words: 76
Prefix code OurBigBook.com
For a success index J with geometric distribution of parameter q=2−n, write J−1=2nQ+R, 0≤R<2n. Encode Q by Q ones followed by zero, then encode R in exactly n bits. This prefix code has length n+Q+1. Since P(Q≥k)=(1−q)k2n, its expected length is the displayed expression, at most n+e/(e−1). Thus a very rare success can be communicated in approximately the logarithm of its inverse probability, rather than one bit per trial.

The prefix tree of a code has vertices corresponding to prefixes of codewords, with one edge for each next symbol. The root represents the empty word. In a prefix code, complete codewords are leaves, and their depths are their codeword lengths.

Undetected error

Binary symmetric channel OurBigBook.com
An error is undetected by codeword-membership checking when the received word is a different valid codeword. For a linear code this occurs exactly when the nonzero channel-error vector is itself a codeword.

Binary symmetric channel OurBigBook.com
At crossover probability p=1/2, the two rows of the transition matrix of a binary symmetric channel coincide. Its output is then independent of its input and its capacity is zero.

If p<1/4, choose p<δ<1/4. Binary codes of relative minimum distance above 2δ have positive asymptotic rate by a greedy packing bound, and nearest-codeword decoding fails only when more than δn channel errors occur. That probability tends to zero.

Maximum a posteriori decoding chooses the codeword maximizing prior probability times channel likelihood and minimizes average decision error.

Minimum-distance decoding chooses a codeword closest to the received word; on a binary symmetric channel with p<1/2, it is maximum-likelihood decoding under Hamming distance.

Bounded-distance decoding

Words: 61
Minimum-distance decoding OurBigBook.com
For a code of minimum Hamming distance d and radius t with 2t<d, bounded-distance decoding returns the unique codeword within Hamming distance t of the received word, or reports failure if none exists. The disjointness of radius-t Hamming balls gives uniqueness. It guarantees recovery when at most t errors occurred, but a word produced by more errors can be nearer to a different codeword and be miscorrected.
